# Game workload results (generated by `benches/game`)

Sources: `game-baseline.jsonl`, `game-final.jsonl` (generated, never hand-edited; summary produced by `novadb-game-bench --summarize`). Machine: 13th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i5-13420H, 12 hardware threads, 23 GiB RAM, Linux 7.0.11-76070011-generic.

## Methodology

* Generator: `benches/game` (Rust/tokio, own MySQL client). P simulated players, each acting every 100-1000 ms (uniform think time, mean 550 ms, so offered load is about P/0.55 ops/s) after a random start offset; closed loop per player (a player waits for its answer before thinking again).
* Mix: 25% character load (`SELECT *` wide row by PK), 25% inventory list (by indexed character_id), 10% quest load, 15% position/stat UPDATE by id, 4% inventory INSERT, 4% UPDATE, 2% DELETE, 5% chat INSERT, 5% leaderboard (`ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 100`, indexed), 5% login (SELECT by username + UPDATE last_login; one sample covers both statements).
* Data set: 100k characters/accounts, 300k quest rows, 1M inventory rows, 2M chat rows (synthetic; schema inspired by a game DB, no real data).
* `pool`: pool-size connections shared by all players (latency includes waiting for a free pooled connection; `wait p99` shows that part). `per-player`: one TCP connection per player. `binary`: COM_STMT_PREPARE once per connection then COM_STMT_EXECUTE; `text`: COM_QUERY with literal SQL. Strings are sent as VAR_STRING (also DATETIME values).
* Server RSS/threads are the maximum of /proc samples every 250 ms in the measured window; server CPU is user+sys of the server process divided by wall time. Client and server share this machine (loopback), so they compete for CPU; the generator runs on 4 tokio worker threads. Results are single-machine, noisy (+-20-30%), and `n` rounds are medians when more than one round is present.
* Latency is measured by the client from just before the first statement of the operation to the last packet of the response.

## What the labels mean

* `baseline`: release build of commit 02bfbdf (0.2.1) before any change in this work. `final`: this working tree (gateway plan cache, bound prepared statements, buffered I/O, per-thread session runtimes, inline reads) on top of the core in the same tree.
* Baseline cells are 3 rounds for P >= 1000 and 1 round for P = 200; final cells have 3 or 4 rounds for P >= 1000 (the pool cells were re-run after a harness port collision, see Caveats). Medians are shown. Data directory on the regular disk (not tmpfs) for both.
* Rows for `sat-*` (see `game-saturated.jsonl`, 3 rounds, 256 players, pool of 64, **no think time**, data on tmpfs) measure capacity of the mixed workload instead of latency under the realistic arrival rate.

## Reading the numbers

* With 100-1000 ms think time the offered load is P/0.55 ops/s. Up to P = 3000 (about 5.5k ops/s) both builds keep up, so ops/s is the same by construction; the gain shows up as server CPU per operation (baseline: not recorded in the first matrix; the tool did not yet compute it. Baseline CPU cores: 1.33 at P=3000 pool binary vs 0.93 final) and as latency. At P = 10000 (18.2k ops/s offered) the baseline pool setup saturated on some rounds (median 15.2k ops/s) and the final build kept up (median 18.3k ops/s) with fewer CPU cores (2.7 vs 3.6).
* Closed-loop capacity (`sat-*`, same mix): baseline 18.2k ops/s (binary) / 18.2k (text) vs final 22.8k / 22.2k ops/s medians, server CPU per operation 330 -> 220 us (binary) and 329 -> 230 us (text). Individual rounds vary by +-20% on this shared machine (ranges in the JSONL).
* Tail latency (p99, max) in the realistic cells is dominated by scheduling noise of a single box that also runs the generator and a desktop session; do not read single p99 values (they differ by 10x between rounds of the same build). p50 is stable.
* Per-player mode at P = 10000 runs 10,000 SQLite connections (about 1.3 MB each, 12-13 GB RSS) and is bounded by memory and thread creation, not by the gateway hot path: 6-10k ops/s in both builds. Pooling (`--mode pool`) is the architecture that scales; see "Remaining bottleneck".

## Where time went (baseline, instrumented build, microseconds per COM_QUERY / COM_STMT_EXECUTE)

Closed loop, 1 connection (no queueing), data on disk, mixed workload. The timers were temporary and are removed.

| Stage | binary | text | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| whole command (after the packet was read, until the response was flushed) | 430 | 482 | includes the awaits below |
| tokenize (`parse_sql`) | 0 | 10 | prepared statements tokenize once at PREPARE |
| translate (`substitute`, `rewrite_*`, `expressions`, render) | 31 | 31 | every execution; prepared statements cloned the token vector first (+5) |
| blocking-pool hop (`run_db` total minus work inside the closure) | about 38 per call, 1.28 calls per command | same | one `spawn_blocking` per statement plus one more for the type lookup |
| database call inside the closure (core) | 198 | 222 | reads 222 us avg and writes 128 us avg in this 1-connection run, including core's own literal normalisation and statement preparation; core micro-benchmark: `SELECT .. WHERE id = <literal>` 21 us, the same text again 10 us, leaderboard 76 us, literal UPDATE 53-61 us |
| result typing (`declared_types`: extra `sqlite_schema` query per SELECT) | 26 | 30 | one more blocking-pool round trip; 50-200 us under load |
| result set conversion (`QueryResult` JSON -> cells -> typed columns) | 46 | 43 | JSON object per row, one hash lookup per cell |
| result encoding (`write_outcome`) | 38 | 61 | one `Vec` per row and column definition |
| flush (one `write` syscall) | 23 | 24 | |

Under load (256 closed-loop players on 64 connections) the same per-command total grew to 2.7-3.5 ms, of which 2.4-3.3 ms was waiting for a blocking-pool thread and the connection's core mutex: the gateway's own stages stayed at about 20 us (translate) and 10 us (conversion); the hop and the extra typing query are what scaled with concurrency.

Other findings: `perf`, `strace -p` and `gdb` are not available here (ptrace is restricted); `strace -c -f` of the server showed `futex` at 87-92% of syscall time in the baseline (blocking-pool hand-offs and work stealing), 300k futex calls for 45k statements.

## Optimisations kept (each verified with the generator, see per-operation closed-loop table)

| Change | Effect (closed loop, 64 players on 8 connections, ops/s baseline -> final, medians of 4 s runs on tmpfs; machine noise +-15%) |
|---|---|
| plan cache (text and prepared), bound parameters, typing cache, no extra query per SELECT | char_load 52k -> 155k, inv_list 26k -> 164k, quest_load 14k -> 214k, pos_update 10k -> 48k, chat_insert 17k -> 37-56k |
| session runtimes + inline cheap reads | `SELECT 1` 103k -> 217-260k (protocol overhead only); server CPU 31 -> 17-20 us per op |
| buffered reads (one `read` per command), rows/column definitions encoded straight into the output buffer, one `write` per response | included above (not separable) |
| `LIMIT`/`OFFSET` values are kept literal in the SQL text instead of bound | core micro-benchmark: `ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 100` over the 100k-row index takes 74 us with a literal and 101 us with `LIMIT ?1` (SQLite plans it worse) |

Variants compared at P = 3000 (pool, binary, data on tmpfs, 2 rounds each): shared runtime with every statement on the blocking pool (`NOVADB_MYSQL_WORKERS=0 NOVADB_MYSQL_INLINE_US=0`), 12 session runtimes with inline reads, 6 and 4 session runtimes. All kept up with the offered 5.5k ops/s; p99 ranged from 2 to 66 ms between rounds of the same variant, i.e. below the noise floor, so this test could not rank them. The shipped default (workers = CPU count, inline below 100 us) was chosen from the closed-loop results, where it was fastest (CPU per op 17-20 us vs 31 us for `SELECT 1`, and the largest gain for cheap reads). One run on the regular disk showed second-long stalls for the shared-runtime variant with inline reads (`WORKERS=0`, `INLINE_US=100`); it did not reproduce on tmpfs, but it is the reason inline reads are paired with per-thread runtimes by default.

## Remaining bottleneck

At 10,000 players in pool mode the server uses about 2.7 CPU cores of the 12 hardware threads that the generator and desktop also use; per operation it spends about 160 us CPU, of which about 45% is system time (loopback `read`/`write`/futex). The remaining gateway-side costs are the JSON row representation returned by core (`Value::Object` per row, then converted to cells), the per-statement mutex and prepare in core, and writes waiting for group commit (50-60 us each). Two core changes would remove most of what is left; see the final report.

## Caveats

* One machine, client and server on the same box and the same cores, a desktop session running; numbers are lower bounds for dedicated hardware and noisy.
* The first full final matrix had its second invocation start the server on a port that was in the ephemeral client range and refused connections for all pool cells of that invocation (6 cells with 0 ops/s); those cells were removed from the file and re-run with a fixed harness (`run.sh` now picks ports below 28000 and waits for the MySQL port). No other cells were removed.
* No real game data was used; the data set is synthetic (100k characters, 300k quest rows, 1M inventory rows, 2M chat rows). Statement shapes and column types were modelled on the table definitions of the user's game schema.
* The generator is a deliberately minimal client (no TLS, `mysql_native_password` with an empty password); real drivers add their own overhead.
